questions.stem: A molecule list reads: glucose, maltose, starch, cellulose. Which family do all four belong to, and what changes along the list?

options.text: Carbohydrates; the molecules grow from single units to very long chains
options.explanation: All four are carbohydrates and the list runs by increasing chain length.

options.text: Lipids; they grow from oils to fats
options.explanation: None of the four is a lipid.

options.text: Proteins; they grow by adding amino acids
options.explanation: None of the four is a protein.

options.text: A mixed list with no single family

questions.stem: State the three chemical elements carbohydrates contain.
Name the polysaccharide that plants use for storage and the one animals use.
questions.modelAnswer: Plants store starch; animals store glycogen.

questions.stem: Explain why cellulose, starch and glycogen can all be built from the same single unit yet play different roles.
questions.modelAnswer: All three are long chains of glucose units, but chain length, the way chains branch and where they are placed differ, so the same building block yields a wall material in plants, a plant energy store and an animal energy store.

questions.stem: An athlete's trainer suggests a slow-release carbohydrate meal before a long race. Using chain length, explain which family member fits that description.
questions.modelAnswer: A long-chain polysaccharide such as starch fits: its large insoluble molecules must be broken down step by step into glucose, releasing energy steadily rather than in one jump the way a drink of simple sugar would.

questions.stem: Name the smaller units proteins are built from.
Give the two smaller units lipids are built from.
Explain why a change in a protein's amino acid sequence can stop the protein doing its job.
questions.modelAnswer: The sequence determines the overall shape of the molecule, and the shape determines what the protein can bind or catalyse; altering the sequence can reshape the working region so it no longer fits its target, leaving the protein unable to function.

questions.stem: A seed contains an energy store and a structural material for new membranes. Which two molecule families and unit pairs should the seed be rich in?
questions.modelAnswer: The energy store should be a lipid (built from glycerol and fatty acids) and the membrane material also draws on lipids, while any growth machinery will need proteins built from amino acids — so the seed banks both families.
